Women are half the people in the world, and black people are maybe a fifth.  (Also I see "African" Natch and "African-American" Slim as being thoroughly different categories of person, no more alike than Legacy and Expatriette.)

The reason why I object to the random "by the way, this character is gay" moments is that it's completely unnecessary to establish any sexuality for a character in a game about battling superheroes.  Gender and race are obvious at a glance, but sexual orientation remains largely invisible unless specifically pointed out (whether in text or in pictures).  We only know of a handful of characters who are explicitly heterosexual - Finest Legacy has a wife, Greatest Legacy probably slept with a woman at least once (in vitro fertilization might have been possible in the first half of the 20th century, but certainly it was less common), Wraith had a boyfriend, and AZ lost a girlfriend, so Tachyon is one gay character in the Freedom V, who contain at least three straight ones (we have no information on Bunker's private life as far as I know).  But for the non-F5 characters, I believe Medico is the only one whose sex life is mentioned in any way; we can presume Omnitronx and Fanatic are functionally asexual, but I don't think there's any information confirming any of the others to be hets.  So why bother confirming one to be gay?  There was no reason why the subject ever needed to be broached.

Rabit:

My nephew has full-on autism, and most autistics do not like contact with people - they just can't stand it. My nephew is completely the opposite: he loves hugs, holding hands, jumping on his uncle's stomach (ugh - he's a heavy kid, takes after his dad). These diseases don't manifest in a "standard" way (unfortunately frown).



I've always found Autism extremely baffling as a concept.  From what I can tell, it seems to be about five hundred different conditions all being considered a single "spectrum" of related diseases, despite there being no single common thread which runs through all of them as far as I've ever heard.  What exactly defines what Autism actually IS?  It's never been explained as far as I can tell.

(The only other word whose definition seems equally confused, as far as I've noticed, is "vampire".  We tend to think we all know what a vampire is, but if you look through all the world mythologies on the topic, there are vampires who don't suck blood, vampires who can go out in the daylight, vampires who aren't dead, vampires who aren't evil, vampires who are or aren't affected by all the classic vampire weaknesses, and even vampires who don't suffer from supernaturally-enforced OCD about rice grains and shoelaces.  Yet despite this lack of a single coherent definition, I have little trouble saying just at a glance, "This is a vampire and that isn't".  For instance, while I can accept that Edward Cullen deserves the title despite how far Stephenee's vampires diverge from the standard, I absolutely draw the line at the "hemophages" from the movie "Ultra-Violet" qualiying as vampires when they possess NONE of the qualifications.  Not a single one; they don't even drink blood, despite the name.  All they have is super-strength and possibly arrested aging…you might as well have called them "supermodels on PCP".)

posts.name: Paul
posts.cooked:
When crafting the bios for SotM characters, any information about their backstory/personal life/etc that "makes the cut" is something that we consider important for the reader to know or understand in order to get a good sense of and feeling for the personality and motivations of the character. However, there are many details about every character that are True, and Canon, but have never yet been revealed. This is either because we are saving the information for a more opportune time, or because it is just not important enough to have come up yet, but may in the future.

Tachyon's sexual orientation is a good example of this phenomenon. Her internal back story had always included her relationship status and sexual orientation, but it happened to not come up until the Freedom Four Annual #1, when there was a plot reason to include some home life scenes from various characters. For Legacy, by contrast, we felt that his relationship status and sexual orientation was more important to understanding his character, so it is alluded to more prominently.

Rest assured, there are a ton of currently unrevealed details about all aspects of all of the characters, from personality traits to disabilities to ethnic backgrounds to preferences of all sorts. Hopefully we'll have the opportunity to eventually share them!

posts.name: Envisioner
posts.cooked:
I definitely favor the idea of heroes of different nationalities, though I'm less fond of them showing up in books published outside the home country of the character...when guys with random accents show up in American comic books, I have a vague sense that the authors are trying to find ways to make a character seem more interesting than they actually are, so they don't have to write as hard, and the results can get a little silly (X-Men was a massive case of this, with Banshee and Colossus and Nightcrawler and several others all speaking in different accents, all comically exagerrated for the sake of text).  But just in the sense of giving a sense of a larger world, I approve of it.

As I said before, bringing sexual orientations into it bugs me because it's not necessary; the setting is not about sex, we don't really need to know that kind of detail about characters' personal lives (I know that comic books are sort of soap-opera-ish, but that's due to the volume they work in, it doesn't need to apply on the scale where SOTM is working).  Additionally, I feel as if just randomly slapping a "gay" tag on a character, without them being in any way different otherwise, is dishonest characterization; an individual ought to be holistic, with every part of who they are being reflected in every other part, even if we never learn all those details.  If the Argent Adept were revealed to be queer, I wouldn't bat an eye, because he plays a freaking flute and flies around in a totally eye-catching, not-at-all-manly costume.  It would fit the character smoothly.  Conversely, if someone as ultra-butch as Char or Citizen Anvil is gay, it seems in-character there too.  But for a character who "just is", and secretly happens to be gay without it altering their personality in any way from the heteronormative male standard...that I don't really buy.  Granted, it's much too soon to know that this is actually the case with Medico; maybe once I start reading his flavor text, it'll be completely obvious that he totally had to be homosexual all along.  But if not, I'll be left with the impression that it was a forced, gratuitous aspect that was stapled onto the character after he'd been fully conceptualized without that detail, and I regard that as a sad failure on a writer's behalf, whether the missing detail is sexuality, or religion, or job preference, or anything else that should have been factored into their persona all along.

posts.cooked:
Envisioner:

As I said before, bringing sexual orientations into it bugs me because it's not necessary; the setting is not about sex, we don't really need to know that kind of detail about characters' personal lives (I know that comic books are sort of soap-opera-ish, but that's due to the volume they work in, it doesn't need to apply on the scale where SOTM is working).  Additionally, I feel as if just randomly slapping a "gay" tag on a character, without them being in any way different otherwise, is dishonest characterization; an individual ought to be holistic, with every part of who they are being reflected in every other part, even if we never learn all those details.  If the Argent Adept were revealed to be queer, I wouldn't bat an eye, because he plays a freaking flute and flies around in a totally eye-catching, not-at-all-manly costume.  It would fit the character smoothly.  Conversely, if someone as ultra-butch as Char or Citizen Anvil is gay, it seems in-character there too.  But for a character who "just is", and secretly happens to be gay without it altering their personality in any way from the heteronormative male standard…that I don't really buy.  Granted, it's much too soon to know that this is actually the case with Medico; maybe once I start reading his flavor text, it'll be completely obvious that he totally had to be homosexual all along.  But if not, I'll be left with the impression that it was a forced, gratuitous aspect that was stapled onto the character after he'd been fully conceptualized without that detail, and I regard that as a sad failure on a writer's behalf, whether the missing detail is sexuality, or religion, or job preference, or anything else that should have been factored into their persona all along.

First, in at least one miniscule aspect, you're right:  this is a superhero game, not a sex game.  Which is why, on cards and in text, we see our heroes beating up villains, saving innocents, and working together as a team for truth and justice rather than watching Legacy get spanked or Nightmist as a dominatrix.  You're not being exposed to any hero's actions in the bedroom. 

Christopher and his crew have gone the extra mile in terms of worldbuilding by making heroes that didn't exist before 2010 or so feel as rich and storied as characters that have been in existence since the 1960s (or long before!).  Part of doing such means doing careful, nuanced characterization.  And, whether you like it or not, that means attaching history and backstory to each character that makes them feel like a fully-developed character.  "Tactfully avoiding" the issue of a hero's sexuality isn't a mature attitude to take, as it leaves out an entire important facet of character.  When you're building a whole Multiverse, you have to consider these characters as whole people.

Let's take, for example, Young Legacy.  There's nothing that's been stated about her sexuality so far, but the inclusion of a dynamic as nuanced as sexual preference provides a platform for character development.  What happens if Young Legacy is a lesbian?  Her powers are passed on by genetics.  Would she be willing to end the Legacy line to live an honest, free life?  I'm not saying that this is the direction that >G should go, but rather it's an entire plot-line of possibility that could not potentially exist without open, frank discussion of sexuality.

I'm going to call a spade a spade here and say outright that your viewpoints on what "should be" and "should not be" acceptable in an LGBT character is homophobic, wrong-headed, and backwards.  Your examples rely on overblown, misrepresented stereotypes (Argent Adept as the unmanly bard, playing a "girl's" instrument, the flute; Char and Mainstay as burly bears) and your statements bely fear of the unknown:  the "hidden" homosexual, out to ruin, to jump out and corrupt, malign, and seduce.  That's pure, unmitigated homophobia.

Why do you feel that there has to be a justification for Medico being gay?  That's unrealistic and unreasonable.  He's gay.  He has a partner and an adopted (superhuman) child.  What more needs be said?  No one has to justify their sexual preference to you or anyone else.  And, for what reason do you think that his sexuality was a "forced, gratuitious aspect that was stapled onto the character after he'd been fully conceptualized…" ?  There's no indication or evidence that his sexuality was an afterthought.  Rather, the fact that his interpersonal relationships develop overtime indicate that there's a greater plan going on–almost as if his writers knew that he was gay from the start.  Huh.  How about that?

You sought to raise my own preferences briefly after I mentioned that I'm both bisexual and I have a wife.  Both statements are correct:  I am a bisexual man married to a wonderful woman (who also happens to be bisexual/bi-curious).  Believe it or not–whether you'd like to admit it or not–I'm one of thousands in that situation:  a bisexual in a long-term relationship that appears, to all outside appearances, to be straight.  I'm also a high school teacher, a published writer and game designer, a fan of Pittsburgh Steelers football, a comic book nerd, and pretty reasonable cook.  All of these are a part of me, yet none specifically define me.  I am, as you are, a sum of my experiences.  Further, I (and pretty much every other member of the LGBT community) don't adhere to a series of outdated, homophobic stereotypes.  My sexuality is a part of who I am, but it is not what defines me.  And you certainly wouldn't be able to tell that I'm bisexual by passing me on the street; I'm no stereotype.

You know what would be gratuitious and unnecessary in SotM?  If the creators chose to make their gay character "Queer-Mo":  a burly man in a leather harness and pink tutu who flings razor-sharp pink triangles at his foes.  The stereotypes that you're specifically choosing to (wrongfully) uphold are absurd and overblown.  No LGBT person wants this as a superhero.  No person wants this as a superhero.  Rather, I (and I think pretty much anyone, really) would much prefer a mature, reasonable take on a hero's personality–if that take includes their sexuality as a part of them, so be it.  

The fact that >G has taken up that viewpoint and dealt with it with maturity–Tachyon's sexuaility is a part of her, not what defines her; same with Medico–makes me proud, as it epitomizes everything that is right and reasonable about the LGBT rights movement.

First, I want to thank everyone for keeping this conversation civil. It's far too easy for this kind of discussion to get out of control, and we really don't want to see that happen.

The only other contribution I want to make is to point out one thing: The way in which the characters of the Multiverse are represented is realistic. We don't have stereotypical representations of race, gender, sexuality, etc.; we have interesting characters. As in real life.

Some folks might not appreciate this, and that's their perogative. But for the folks who do, this is often a very big deal (as we can see from the examples provided so far in this thread). We should respect each other's views, learn from them, and - sometimes - just accept that we aren't going to agree.

Keep on saving the Multiverse!
